title: Rootstock Effects on Yield Efficiency, Leaf Gas Exchange and Photochemical Performance of Bergamot (Citrus bergamia Risso & Poit.) Under High Evaporative Demand
content: Bergamot (Citrus bergamia Risso & Poit.) is grown almost exclusively along a narrow coastal strip of southern Calabria (southern Italy), an area increasingly exposed to severe summer drought. In a commercial orchard, ‘Femminello’ trees grafted onto sour orange (Citrus aurantium L.; SO), Troyer citrange [Poncirus trifoliata (L.) Raf. × Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck; TC] and Volkamer lemon (Citrus volkameriana Ten. & Pasq.; VL) were compared over two seasons (2025–2026) for canopy growth, yield, leaf gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence and leaf water potential; sap flow was monitored with the heat ratio method and wood integrity was assessed by electrical resistivity tomography. SO and VL gave cumulative yields that did not differ significantly (313 and 281 kg tree⁻¹) and higher net assimilation rates than TC. VL developed the largest canopy and reached the same cumulative yield efficiency as SO (2.73 kg cm⁻²), with alternate bearing and gas exchange similar to those of SO, the lowest sap flow velocity and the highest effective quantum yield of PSII (ΦPSII). TC combined the largest trunk with the lowest yield and yield efficiency (−37%), the strongest alternate bearing, the lowest net assimilation and stomatal conductance, and the highest sap flow velocity. Taken together with the principal component analysis, these results indicate that Volkamer lemon, which is tolerant to Citrus tristeza virus (CTV), is a promising alternative to sour orange for new bergamot orchards under increasing evaporative demand.
